english: Let $L_1$ be the line through the point $(2,1,2)$ parallel to the vector $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$, and let $L_2$ be the line through the point $(0,-1,-2)$ parallel to the vector $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$. The locus of a point of the $xy$-plane which is equidistant from $L_1$ and $L_2$ meets the $x$-axis only at $(\alpha,0,0)$ and the $y$-axis only at $(0,\beta,0)$. Then the value of $\alpha+\beta$ is ______.
hindi: माना कि $L_1$ बिन्दु $(2,1,2)$ से होकर जाने वाली तथा सदिश $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}+2\hat{k}$ के समान्तर रेखा है, तथा $L_2$ बिन्दु $(0,-1,-2)$ से होकर जाने वाली तथा सदिश $\hat{i}+2\hat{j}-2\hat{k}$ के समान्तर रेखा है। $xy$-तल के उस बिन्दु का बिन्दुपथ, जो $L_1$ तथा $L_2$ से समदूरस्थ है, $x$-अक्ष से केवल $(\alpha,0,0)$ पर तथा $y$-अक्ष से केवल $(0,\beta,0)$ पर मिलता है। तब $\alpha+\beta$ का मान ______ है।
solution: For $P(x,y,0)$, distance$^2$ from a line through $A$ along $\overrightarrow{u}$: $|\overrightarrow{AP}|^2-\dfrac{(\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{u})^2}{|\overrightarrow{u}|^2}$
The quadratic terms cancel because $\overrightarrow{u}$, $\overrightarrow{v}$ have the same $x$, $y$ components: $d_1^2-d_2^2=\dfrac{-8x-4y-8}{3}=0\Rightarrow 2x+y+2=0$
A straight line in the $xy$-plane: $\alpha=-1$, $\beta=-2$, so $\alpha+\beta=-3$
solution_full: For a point $P$ and a line through $A$ with direction $\overrightarrow{u}$, the foot of the perpendicular splits $\overrightarrow{AP}$ into a part along $\overrightarrow{u}$ of length $\dfrac{|\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{u}|}{|\overrightarrow{u}|}$ and a perpendicular part, so the distance $d$ satisfies $d^2=|\overrightarrow{AP}|^2-\dfrac{(\overrightarrow{AP}\cdot\overrightarrow{u})^2}{|\overrightarrow{u}|^2}$.

Equidistance ($d_1=d_2$, equivalently $d_1^2=d_2^2$) gives $2x+y+2=0$: in the $xy$-plane the locus is this straight line. The $x^2$, $y^2$, $xy$ terms cancelled because the directions differ only in the sign of the $z$-component.
It meets the $x$-axis only at $x=-1$ and the $y$-axis only at $y=-2$, so $\alpha=-1$, $\beta=-2$ and $\alpha+\beta=-3$.
originality_note: New: points of a coordinate plane equidistant from two skew lines whose directions are mirror images in that plane; the quadratic parts of the two point-line distances cancel, so the planar locus is a straight line (way 4: hidden symmetry). Closest known: locus of points equidistant from two given points (perpendicular bisector) or from two intersecting lines in a plane. Different because: the lines are skew, the distance to each is a quadratic expression, and the cancellation is what must be discovered.

concept_use.Locus problems in three dimensions: The distance of a general point of the xy-plane from each 3D line is written by the projection formula, and the equidistance condition is set up as a locus in space restricted to z = 0.
concept_use.Locus based questions: The equation in x, y simplifies to the straight line 2x + y + 2 = 0, read in the coordinate plane through its intercepts (2D locus).

stem_review: Read as a student: every point, line, vector and plane is introduced before use, every condition is stated, each sentence has one reading; the answer was recomputed independently with sympy/numpy, is unique and equals the Answer Plan. Avoided saying in the stem that the locus is a straight line (said only that it meets each axis at one point) so the cancellation is not revealed; both intercepts are unique. Changed: removed 'is a straight line' from an earlier draft.
key_step: Writing the squared distance from (x, y, 0) to each line and noticing that the quadratic parts cancel, leaving a straight line.
justification: Two ideas linked: the point-to-line distance in space for a general point, and a 2D locus whose linearity depends on a hidden symmetry of the directions; exact algebra with no options. Comparable to the 3D foot-of-perpendicular work of 2026-P2-Q7 (L3).
